title: Anthropology

paragraphs.text: Ethnography is based on the apparently simple idea that in order to understand what people are up to, it is best to observe them by interacting with them closely, and over an extended period. That is why anthropologists have traditionally tended to spend long periods – sometimes years at a stretch – living in communities they study, sharing the lives of the people as much as possible. To the cultural or social anthropologist, ethnography is what laboratory work is to the biologist, what archival research is to the historian, or what survey research is to the sociologist. It is the focus on ethnography that has defined anthropology, and distinguished it from other disciplines.

Anthropologists certainly do not dismiss the methods which are more characteristic of other disciplines, such as the use of questionnaires or the collection of quantitative behavioural data. But anthropologists have long felt that approaching the study of human beings in those ways is likely to produce an incomplete – even misleading – understanding of the people being studied, especially when those people are members of foreign or unfamiliar societies.

It might also be said that fieldwork is what gives anthropology a good deal of its romance. Today, Western anthropologists conduct fieldwork in settings that are as ordinary as television stations in city centres, magistrates' courts in small towns, and boardrooms in corporate headquarters. But in its infancy as a profession, anthropology was distinguished by its concentration on so-called 'primitive' societies: relatively small communities in which social institutions appeared to be fairly limited and simple, which turned out not to be the case. Such societies, it was felt, provided anthropologists with a simplified view of the 'elementary' workings of society, one that contrasted with the 'complexities' of a modern society.

Early anthropologists appeared to be in a hurry. There was a sense among them that the ways of life represented by these smaller societies were rapidly disappearing. Also, since many of these societies had no writing, the task of preserving a record for posterity was considered urgent. This orientation of the discipline, and an early commitment to the first-hand collection of ethnographic data, led anthropologists to some of the most remote and exotic places on earth.

Most often working alone, and in isolation from other Westerners, the anthropologist is very noticeable. Often this isolation creates a sense of alienation and loneliness, especially in the early stages of fieldwork. But almost all anthropologists eventually find themselves assimilating the culture of their host communities to a greater or lesser degree. In fact, leaving the field can be almost as difficult as entering it; considering the effort required to become established in a community, parting company with friends and now-familiar ways of life can be a painful experience. A few never return home. All in all, fieldwork can be a challenging and unique experience, one that continues to attract men and women to anthropology. It also happens that ethnography seems to be the most effective way of understanding the ways in which other people view the world and interact with it, and it often provides a check on the anthropologist's own preoccupations and beliefs.

It should be obvious that a truly comprehensive description of any society's culture is far beyond the capacity of even a hundred researchers, let alone one. An anthropologist goes to the field with the intention of studying some particular aspect of social life. He or she does not enter into the project unprepared. What anthropologists need to know is as diverse and varied as the studies they undertake. Most begin their preparation with several years of study of the history and previous ethnographic literature of the region in which they propose to do fieldwork. Because anthropologists have felt it essential that they conduct their fieldwork in the language of the people they study, without using translators, they may need to acquire reasonable fluency in several languages. In addition to such general preparation, anthropologists are usually trained in more specialised fields concerning the kind of subject they intend to investigate. A researcher who intends to study the medicinal use of plants among an Amazonian people, for example, needs to learn not only a good deal of conventional botany, but also needs to be familiar with how various of the world's peoples have categorised and used plants.

Dialogue is the backbone of ethnographical research. While anthropologists make use of a variety of techniques to elicit and record data, the interview is by far the most important. Interviews can range in formality from a highly structured question-and-answer session with a local specialist, to the recording of an individual's life history, to informal conversations, or to a brief exchange during an unexpected encounter. Ultimately, the key to ethnographic success is being there, available to observe, available to follow up, available to take advantage of the situation. Beyond the apparently simple techniques of interview and dialogue, anthropologists also employ a variety of more specialised techniques: audio recording of speech and music, photography, mapping, census taking, archival research, and collecting botanical or other natural samples. They all have their uses, depending on the specific research project.

options.text: rejecting a commonly held view about ethnography
contrasting the aims of anthropologists and sociologists
explaining the working methods of anthropologists
describing a personal experience of studying communities

questions.prompt: According to the writer, why did early anthropologists feel they had no time to lose?

options.text: Working in remote areas would get more difficult as they got older.
The societies they wanted to study were changing.
Written records were rapidly being destroyed.
They wanted to be the first to reach isolated communities.

questions.prompt: In the fifth paragraph, what does the writer suggest about the work of anthropologists in remote areas?

options.text: The challenges discourage others from taking up the profession.
The benefits do not justify the difficulties that individuals face.
Individuals gradually adjust to the situation they are working in.
Host communities generally appreciate the interest in their culture.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about ethnography in the fifth paragraph?

options.text: It may lead anthropologists to revise their own view of the world.
It helps to confirm researchers' preconceptions about other communities.
It can sometimes lead anthropologists to draw false conclusions.
It requires researchers to present their findings in a clear context.

subtitle: It has often been said that if you want to understand what anthropology is, you should look at what anthropologists do. And what anthropologists do above all else is ethnography
